candidateRows: The biological orientation of pain and pleasure is more expected on naturalism than on theism.
It supplies the first of three independent comparative-probability arguments supporting the claimed evidential advantage of naturalism.
After defining naturalism, Schieber compares what naturalism and theism lead observers to expect about pain and pleasure serving biological rather than primarily moral goals.
The prevalence and distribution of sentient languishing fit naturalism better than they fit theism.
It establishes the second independent body of suffering-related facts alleged to favor naturalism over theism.
Schieber develops facts about competition, scarce resources, and the small proportion of sentient beings that flourish, then compares their expectedness under both hypotheses.
The occurrence of horrendous evils is substantially less surprising on naturalism than on theism.
It provides the third independent evidential line and directly applies the comparative argument to the most severe forms of suffering.
Schieber defines horrendous evil, contrasts indifferent natural processes with a perfectly knowledgeable and compassionate deity, and argues that such evil favors naturalism.
Schieber has not shown that naturalism itself predicts any of the three cited classes of suffering facts.
It attacks the naturalistic likelihood component shared by all three of Schieber's comparative evidential arguments.
Schieber's claim that naturalism predicts biological pain, widespread languishing, and horrendous evil better than theism.

Bertuzzi challenges the biological analogy and argues that placing evolutionary processes or behavioral tendencies in background knowledge either helps both hypotheses or leaves naturalism without explanatory resources.
Soul-building makes suffering at least as probable on theism as it is on naturalism.
The move directly advances the principal no-evidence defense by attempting to neutralize the comparative likelihood advantage claimed for naturalism.
Schieber's three arguments that biologically useful pain, sentient languishing, and horrendous evil are less expected on theism.
Bertuzzi argues that significant suffering enables valuable loving virtues, can be integrated into a good life and ultimately defeated, and may occupy a narrowly suitable virtue-forming range.
Skeptical theism blocks the inference to naturalism because theism's probability for the suffering data is unknown.
It offers an independent defeater intended to deny the comparative conclusion even if the naturalistic prediction and soul-building disputes are resolved against him.
Schieber's inference that a higher likelihood of the suffering data on naturalism establishes evidential support over theism.
Bertuzzi invokes the epistemic gap between humans and divinity, possible unknown or incomprehensibly complex goods, and the missing premise that theism fails to predict the data.
Comparative evidence requires only that naturalism predict the facts better than theism, and the pain analogy remains inductively sound.
The reply defends both the operative comparative-likelihood standard and the inferential basis of the first evidential argument.
Bertuzzi's objection that naturalism must independently predict biologically oriented pain and that Schieber's bodily-system analogy is invalid.

Schieber clarifies that naturalism need only outperform theism rather than make the facts probable in isolation, then argues that the compressor example illustrates defeasible but legitimate induction.
Evolutionary background knowledge does not entail widespread languishing, which therefore remains a better fit with naturalism.
The move repairs a conceded technical defect while preserving the second major comparative evidential argument.
Bertuzzi's claim that including evolutionary competition in background knowledge causes both naturalism and theism to predict the languishing data.
Schieber narrows the relevant evolutionary background to common descent and genetic change, observes that these do not entail his flourishing facts, and restores the likelihood comparison.
Morally blind natural forces make horrendous evil less surprising than it is under theistic background assumptions.
It defends the third principal evidential argument by restating the relevant contrast as comparative surprise rather than entailment.
Bertuzzi's demand for an explanation of how naturalism predicts that people act horribly or undergo extreme suffering.
Schieber argues that the issue is comparative surprise: indifferent processes need not respect personal psychological limits, whereas horrendous evil is puzzling against theistic expectations.
The biological orientation and moral randomness of pain and pleasure remain more expected on naturalism than on a soul-building form of theism.
This directly defends the first evidential comparison in Justin's case by arguing that soul-building does not raise the theistic expectation of the observed system.
Cameron's claim that soul-building makes the pain-and-pleasure evidence comparably expected on theism.
Justin argues that the observed pain-and-pleasure system is strongly organized around biological goals while remaining morally random, which makes soul-building a particularly poor answer.
A human-focused soul-building account cannot explain most sentient flourishing and languishing, and God could achieve character formation through less harmful means.
The move attacks both the scope and necessity of the proposed theodicy, preserving the evidential force of nonhuman suffering and avoidable human suffering.
Cameron's proposal that suffering is required for soul-building goods such as courage, empathy, and forgiveness.
Justin contends that humans form only a small part of sentient history and that transformative dreams or visions could produce moral growth without comparable real-world harms.
Horrendous evils are soul-destroying rather than soul-building, and a perfectly empathic and resourceful God would have decisive reason to prevent them.
This move directly supports a principal evidential category by arguing that horrendous suffering is substantially more surprising under morally perfect theism.
Cameron's use of soul-building to neutralize the evidential significance of horrendous and apparently destructive evils.
Justin argues that horrendous evils inflict severe moral injury and that an unsurpassably empathic God could secure soul-building and knowledge of God without permitting them.
Skeptical theism does not favor permission over prevention because unknown moral reasons may count in either direction, leaving known reasons to break the tie.
This challenges the principal epistemic defense offered to neutralize all three categories of evil evidence rather than addressing only one local example.
Cameron's skeptical-theist claim that human inability to discern God's reasons prevents evil from counting against theism.
Justin grants that unknown justifying reasons may exist but argues that unknown reasons against permission are equally possible, so the known evidence retains comparative force.
Justin has supplied no reliable naturalistic expectation for the evil data because his analogical inference is contestable and his background knowledge is selectively restricted.
The argument disputes the naturalistic side of the central likelihood comparison and concludes that the evidence may surprise both hypotheses without favoring either.
Justin's claim that biological systems and evolutionary background knowledge make the observed evil data more expected on naturalism.
Cameron argues that defeasibility does not establish a good inference, offers an alternative assignment of biological and moral roles, and says parallel possibilities undermine Justin's comparison.
Soul-building can accommodate pain, nonhuman suffering, and horrendous evil while a fine-tuning argument from saint-producing badness may affirmatively favor theism.
This is Cameron's comprehensive defense of the principal theodicy and culminates in the stronger claim that the observed ensemble of evil can confirm theism.
Justin's objections that soul-building fails for biologically oriented pain, nonhuman languishing, alternative means, and horrendous evil.
Cameron defends morally significant freedom, extends soul-building to animals and an afterlife, rejects dreams as equally effective, disputes permanent soul destruction, and invokes fine-tuning.
Skeptical-theist agnosticism is not an appeal to a favorable pool of unknown reasons, and limited known evidence cannot properly defeat the underlying lack of information.
The move defends the global epistemic defeater intended to block any inference from the evil data to naturalism's comparative confirmation.
Justin's contention that unknown reasons cancel out and that the known reasons therefore break the tie against theism.
Cameron distinguishes agnosticism from hypothesizing unknown justifiers and argues that an unrepresentative, radically limited sample cannot warrant confidence about the whole.
Cameron's alternative does not answer the degree of biological orientation at issue, and mere possibility under evolution does not erase Justin's comparative likelihood arguments.
This defends the naturalistic likelihood comparison against Cameron's two main objections concerning the analogy and the selection of background information.
Cameron's objections that Justin's biological analogy lacks support and that his treatment of background knowledge is arbitrary.
Justin says Cameron confuses moral relevance with actual orientation, explains that evidential arguments require a starting background, and reiterates why biological utility favors naturalism.
Animal afterlife, soul-building narratives, and fine-tuned evil do not explain the observed proportions or justify preventable horrendous harms.
The move answers Cameron's expanded theodicy across flourishing, horrendous evil, afterlife compensation, and the attempted offensive fine-tuning argument.
Cameron's expanded soul-building account involving animal rationality, an afterlife, defeat of suffering, and fine-tuned saint-producing evil.

Justin argues that animal heaven does not predict the relevant proportions, religious experience offers less harmful alternatives, compensation is not justification, and afterlife claims add unsupported detail.
Even if skeptical theism requires agnosticism about theism's predictions, naturalism can still outperform it because naturalism assigns the evil data a comparatively higher likelihood.
This supplies Justin's final answer to the global skeptical-theist defense by distinguishing low confidence from the complete absence of comparative evidential support.
Cameron's analogy that severe informational limits require agnosticism and prevent the available evil data from supporting naturalism.
Using a population-sampling analogy, Justin argues that limited data may still favor one hypothesis over an agnostic rival, so skeptical theism performs poorly relative to naturalism.
Skeptical theism's agnosticism about how probable evil is given theism blocks the inference from naturalism predicting evil to evil confirming naturalism over theism.
This directly addresses whether skeptical theism neutralizes the claimed evidential advantage of naturalism, which is one of the debate motion's principal points of dispute.
Justin Schieber's claim that skeptical theism performs poorly relative to naturalism even if skeptical theism is true.

After finishing his response concerning fine-tuning and the total evidence of evil, Bertuzzi turns to Schieber's two objections to skeptical theism and argues that predictive success for naturalism alone does not establish comparative confirmation.
Bertuzzi concludes that his soul-building and skeptical-theist arguments jointly withstand Schieber's probabilistic argument from evil.
The synthesis states the pro side's ultimate conclusion about the total debate case, tying the preceding soul-building responses and skeptical-theist defense directly to the motion.
Justin Schieber's probabilistic case that facts about evil provide comparative evidence favoring naturalism over theism.

Bertuzzi closes by consolidating the claimed success of his first two responses against the probabilistic problem of evil and his third skeptical-theist argument, emphasizing that the proposed agnosticism remains undefeated.
